Abstract The Indonesian government has designated ten tourist destinations as Muslim-friendly, all of which are situated within Muslim-majority regions. While these initiatives mark significant progress in strengthening halal tourism, there remains a notable research gap concerning the behavioral intentions of Muslim travelers to visit destinations located in non-Muslim areas. This study seeks to address that gap by exploring the key determinants influencing Muslim travelers’ intentions to visit non-Muslim tourism destinations in Indonesia. Integrating the theory of planned behavior (TPB) with the marketing mix framework, this research provides a comprehensive perspective that combines psychological and marketing dimensions of travel decision-making. Data were collected from 361 Muslim respondents through a structured online questionnaire, and the proposed hypotheses were examined using multiple regression analysis. The findings reveal that the main components of TPB—attitude, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control—positively influence travel intention. Likewise, the marketing mix factors —product, price, place, and promotion —also demonstrate a substantial effect on the intention to travel to non-Muslim destinations. Interestingly, religiosity was found to have no significant impact, suggesting that Muslim travelers may prioritize overall travel experiences, accessibility, and service quality over purely religious considerations when choosing destinations. These results highlight the growing openness and adaptability of Muslim tourists as they explore diverse cultural and geographical settings. From a policy perspective, the study emphasizes the importance of governments, tourism authorities, and industry stakeholders extending Muslim-friendly facilities, services, and communication strategies to regions with Muslim-minority populations. Doing so can enhance inclusivity, encourage cross-cultural engagement, and foster a more sustainable and diversified model of halal tourism development in Indonesia and beyond. Keywords: halal tourism, theory of planned behavior, marketing mix, religiosity, travel experience 1. Introduction In global tourism, the rise of halal tourism, also known as Muslim-friendly tourism, has garnered significant interest and discussion among scholars, industry professionals, and policymakers. This rapidly expanding sector, which caters to the specific needs and preferences of Muslim travelers, has become a notable niche within the larger tourism industry (Al-Ansi et al., 2023). Halal tourism aligns with Islamic principles and values, making it a unique segment within the tourism market (Ekka, 2024). With approximately 1.9 billion Muslims worldwide, accounting for nearly a quarter of the global population, there is a growing demand for travel experiences that adhere to Islamic principles (Losurdo, 2022; Rhama, 2022). Recently, Muslim-friendly tourism has gained traction in several Asian countries, including Taiwan, Korea, Japan, and Singapore (Marlinda et al., 2023), as well as in the United Kingdom, Canada, and Spain, where it is also gaining popularity (Ainin et al., 2020). This growth is driven by the increasing number of Muslim travelers visiting these destinations (Samori et al., 2016). Halal tourism encompasses a range of services, including halal-certified accommodations and dining options, prayer facilities, modest dress codes, and gender-segregated amenities, all of which are designed to respect the religious and cultural sensitivities of Muslim travelers. The concept is rooted in the Islamic principles of halal (permissible) and haram (prohibited), which influence many aspects of Muslim life, including food, clothing, behavior, and interactions. Muslim travelers often seek halal food options at their destinations (Akyol & Kilinc, 2014). One of the practical challenges in halal tourism is maintaining halal standards (Boğan & Sarıışık, 2019). In the context of tourism, halal refers to activities, products, and services that comply with Islamic law and ethics, ensuring that they are permissible and free from prohibited elements. This condition encompasses sourcing and preparing food following Islamic dietary laws, as well as providing environments that are suitable for prayer, modesty, and family-oriented activities. Effective management of Muslim-friendly attributes by destination management can enhance tourist engagement and satisfaction (Abror et al., 2021). The intention of Muslim travelers to visit halal or Muslim-friendly destinations is influenced by a complex mix of religious, cultural, economic, social, and experiential factors. The concept of halal encompasses not only the sourcing and preparation of food by Islamic dietary laws but also the provision of accommodations, activities, and services that comply with Islamic ethics and norms. Religious considerations significantly influence the intentions of Muslim travelers to visit Muslim-friendly destinations (Abror et al., 2019; Adel et al., 2021). For devout Muslims, travel is not only a leisure activity but also a spiritual journey of great religious significance. Choosing destinations that adhere to halal practices enables Muslim travelers to fulfil their religious obligations, such as performing daily prayers, fasting during Ramadan, and adhering to modest dress codes while experiencing new cultures. Additionally, visiting places with a strong Islamic heritage and cultural identity allows Muslim travelers to deepen their connection to their faith, thereby enhancing their spiritual experience and fostering a sense of belonging within the global Muslim community. Religiosity has been shown to moderate customer satisfaction with halal tourism (Abror et al., 2019; Liat et al., 2021). From a cultural perspective, halal tourism offers Islamic-friendly programs, services, and facilities. In addition, halal tourism introduces Islamic heritage sites to both Muslim and non-Muslim visitors (Olsen, 2011; Nassar et al., 2015). Cultural affinity and identity play a significant role in Muslim travelers' decisions to choose halal tourism destinations. For many, the motivation to visit places where their cultural heritage and values are respected and celebrated is strong. Whether they explore historical sites, attend cultural events, or interact with local communities, Muslim travelers seek authentic and immersive experiences that align with their cultural identities. Halal tourism destinations that provide opportunities for cultural exchange, interfaith dialogue, and cross-cultural understanding help foster greater cohesion and harmony among diverse communities. Economic factors significantly influence Muslim travelers' intentions to visit halal tourism destinations (Aziz et al., 2018). As the Muslim travel market grows and diversifies, destinations and businesses are increasingly recognizing the economic potential of catering to this segment. The halal tourism sector, which includes halal-certified hotels, restaurants, tour operators, and retailers, offers lucrative market opportunities for stakeholders across the tourism value chain (Ratnasari et al., 2021). Consequently, Muslim travelers are drawn to destinations that offer a range of halal-friendly amenities and services, providing value for money and ensuring a seamless travel experience. Social factors also play a significant role in shaping Muslim travelers' intentions toward halal tourism destinations, particularly family-oriented travel and community engagement. Many Muslim families prioritize destinations offering halal food options, prayer facilities, and family-friendly activities. A strong connection exists between halal tourism and halal entrepreneurship within the halal travel market (Battour et al., 2022). Destinations that cater to the needs of families and provide a safe, welcoming environment for children and elderly travelers are more likely to attract visitors and receive positive word-of-mouth recommendations within the Muslim travel community. Additionally, sense of community and belonging at halal tourism destinations enhances the overall travel experience, creating lasting memories and meaningful connections among travelers. Muslim-friendly tourism appeals not only to Muslim travelers but also to non-Muslim travelers. Experiential motivations drive Muslim travelers toward halal tourism destinations, as they seek unique and memorable experiences that align with their interests and preferences. Both culinary tours featuring halal cuisine, wellness retreats based on Islamic principles, and adventure activities tailored for Muslim travelers, halal tourism destinations offer a diverse range of experiences to suit various tastes. The desire for authentic and immersive experiences encourages Muslim travelers to explore new destinations and engage with local cultures, promoting mutual understanding and respect across cultural and religious boundaries. These experiential motivations stem from excellent service quality, which can enhance tourist value cocreation (Abror et al., 2023). Research on Muslim-friendly tourism has focused primarily on two aspects. The first area of study concentrates on the development of Muslim-friendly tourism in Indonesia. This includes discussions on policies in Indonesia, support from Sharia financial institutions, and marketing efforts by both the private sector and the government to promote Muslim-friendly tourism in the country (Abror et al., 2021; Nugroho et al., 2023; Bahri & Halmahera, 2023; Kurniawati & Fathoni, 2023; Mandalia, 2023; Yahya et al., 2022). The second area of study examines the phenomenon of Muslim-friendly tourism in various Muslim and non- Muslim countries, as well as in different regions of Indonesia, including both Muslim-majority and minority areas. This research explores a range of topics, such as opportunities and challenges, potential, tourist satisfaction, and the development of Muslim- friendly tourism in Muslim-minority countries (Abbas et al., 2023; Eum, 2018; Han et al., 2019; Juliana et al., 2021; Mahliza et al., 2021; Putra et al., 2021; Said et al., 2022; Sutikno et al., 2023). Although considerable research has been conducted on Muslim-friendly or halal tourism, most of it has focused on Muslim destinations. This study, however, examines Muslim tourists' intentions to visit non-Muslim destinations. There is still a need for more research on non-Muslim destinations. Adel et al. (2021) and Aji et al. (2021) investigated the decision-making process of Muslim travelers when visiting non-Muslim destinations, whereas other studies explored the behavior and needs of Muslim travelers in non-Islamic destinations (Hassani & Moghavvemi, 2019; Nassar et al., 2015; Sriprasert et al., 2014). Previous research has focused mainly on non-Muslim countries, but this study centers on Indonesian Muslim travelers visiting non- Muslim destinations within Indonesia. The Indonesian government has designated 10 Muslim-friendly tourist destinations, all in Muslim-majority areas. However, there is potential to develop Muslim-friendly tourism in both Muslim-majority and Muslim-minority areas in https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Arif et al. (2026) 3 Indonesia. The primary distinction between this research and previous studies is that it integrates the theory of planned behavior with the marketing mix to assess Muslim tourists' intention to visit non-Muslim destinations. The combination of theories used is the main novelty of this research compared with previous research. This research aims to identify the factors that influence Muslim tourists' intentions to visit non-Muslim destinations in Indonesia. The findings indicate that Muslim tourists are more likely to visit non-Muslim destinations if these destinations offer Muslim-friendly facilities. This study provides valuable insights into the development of Muslim-friendly tourism in non-Muslim destinations and will assist the Indonesian government in enhancing Muslim-friendly tourism in areas such as North Sulawesi, Bali, and other regions with significant Muslim minority populations. 2. Literature Review 2.1. Muslim-friendly tourism Muslim-friendly tourism, often referred to as halal tourism or Islamic tourism, has experienced significant growth in recent years in response to the increasing demand from Muslim travelers who wish to maintain their religious practices while exploring global destinations (Ainin et al., 2020). This growing segment is driven by several factors, including rising incomes in Muslim-majority countries, increased awareness of religious obligations, and the proliferation of information through digital media. As a result, Muslim travelers are seeking not only pilgrimage destinations such as Makkah and Madinah but also broader leisure experiences that comply with Islamic principles (Battour & Ismail, 2016; Rasul, 2019; Aminudin & Jamal, 2020). Muslim-friendly tourism is not a monolithic concept but rather a multidimensional framework that accommodates the needs of Muslim travelers in areas such as food, accommodations, worship, entertainment, and lifestyle. Essential components of halal tourism include the provision of halal-certified food, gender-segregated recreational facilities, prayer spaces, and the absence of alcohol and gambling-related services (Carboni & Janati, 2016; Battour & Ismail, 2016; Wardi et al., 2018). The goal of Muslim-friendly tourism is to provide inclusive and welcoming experiences that enable Muslim travelers to practice their faith comfortably while exploring destinations worldwide (Mohsin et al., 2016). In many cases, destinations that are not predominantly Muslim majors must adapt their tourism offerings to include these features to attract Muslim tourists and remain competitive in the global market. A major challenge, however, lies in the lack of standardization and clarity in halal certification and the broader framework of what constitutes “Muslim-friendly” services. The diversity of interpretations and practices among Muslim communities globally leads to inconsistency in service delivery and tourists' perceptions (Khan & Callanan, 2017). This ambiguity may cause uncertainty and diminish trust, especially when Muslim travelers visit non-Muslim destinations. As Muslim-friendly tourism continues to evolve, scholars argue that it must be understood not only as a religious requirement but also as a sociocultural and economic phenomenon. The incorporation of ethical consumption, family orientation, and moral values into tourism behaviors distinguishes Muslim travelers from other consumer segments and presents opportunities for further market segmentation and service innovation. 2.2. Theory of planned behaviour This research adopts the theory of planned behavior (TPB) as its primary theoretical framework. Developed by Ajzen (1991), the theory of planned behavior (TPB) is a well-established social psychological theory designed to predict and understand human behavior, particularly in decision-making related to actions under volitional control. The core components of the basic TPB are attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control. In this study, the TPB model is extended by integrating religiosity as a fourth dimension, acknowledging the significance of spiritual and faith-based influences in shaping travel intentions among Muslim tourists, particularly when non-Muslim destinations are considered. Attitude refers to an individual’s positive or negative evaluation of performing a behavior—in this case, travelling to a non-Muslim destination that offers Muslim-friendly facilities. It incorporates both instrumental beliefs (perceived outcomes) and experiential beliefs (emotional responses) toward the behavior (Magnini et al., 2013; Wan et al., 2017). Previous tourism studies have shown that attitude positively influences tourism intentions (Liu et al., 2018; Nursalwani & Zulariff, 2017; Seow et al., 2017; Akter & Hasan, 2023). In the context of halal tourism, attitudes may be shaped by perceived safety, comfort in practicing religious rituals, and the availability of halal services. Subjective norms relate to perceived social pressure from significant others—such as family members, friends, or religious communities—to engage or not engage in a behavior. In collectivist cultures, which are common in Muslim societies, subjective norms often exert a powerful influence on decision-making (Khuram et al., 2021). Studies have demonstrated that approval from referent groups can significantly increase the likelihood of engaging in travel behavior aligned with religious and cultural values (Lam & Hsu, 2006; Saifudin & Puspita, 2020; Ramadhani & Mochklas, 2019; Erul et al., 2023; Nguyen et al., 2023). In the TPB framework, perceived behavioral control (PBC) directly affects behavioral intentions. PBC refers to an individual's perception of how easy or difficult it is to perform a behavior, including factors such as self-efficacy, perceived obstacles, and available resources. Previous research has indicated that PBC influences the intention to visit tourist destinations (Seow et al., 2017; Ramamonjiarivelo et al., 2015; Akter & Hasan, 2023; Lestari et al., 2023). In the context of Muslim-friendly https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Arif et al. (2026) 4 tourism, religiosity serves as a motivational construct that deeply influences how and where Muslim individuals choose to travel. Highly religious individuals may demonstrate greater concern for compliance with Islamic norms when evaluating potential destinations, even at the expense of convenience or cost. Religiosity encompasses the way individuals and societies live in accordance with their religious values and attitudes (El- Gohary, 2016). It reflects the degree to which individuals or communities adhere to, practice, and express their religious beliefs, including rituals, prayers, religious services, and overall engagement with religious activities (Zamami-Farahani & Musa, 2012). The intensity, frequency, and depth of religious involvement can be used to measure religiosity. In the context of Muslim- friendly tourism, religiosity highlights the importance of religious beliefs and practices in shaping travel preferences and decisions within this market segment. 2.3. Marketing mix Tourist intention refers to a traveler's planned or expected behavior regarding visiting a particular destination. To understand the factors influencing Muslim tourists' intention to travel, this study also incorporates marketing mixes (4Ps), such as products, prices, places, and promotions, as a complementary analytical lens. This framework offers a practical perspective for tourism destination marketers and service providers aiming to attract the growing Muslim travel market. Each component can significantly influence tourists' destination choices, especially within niche markets such as Muslim-friendly tourism. In tourism, a product encompasses not only the physical attributes of a destination but also experiences, cultural compatibility, and service offerings. Muslim-friendly tourism includes halal food options, the availability of mosques, and adherence to Islamic values. A well-designed tourism product aligned with Islamic principles can increase perceived value and influence positive travel intentions among Muslim tourists. Pricing plays a pivotal role in shaping tourists’ perceptions of value and affordability. Competitive pricing, particularly for halal-compliant packages, can act as an incentive for travel decisions. In a cost-sensitive market segment, travelers may compare value-added services, such as religious compliance, with pricing models offered by competing destinations (Battour et al., 2018). Moreover, transparent and fair pricing, coupled with price bundling for Muslim travelers, enhances trust and travel intentions. Place refers not only to the destination itself but also to the ease of access, convenience, and availability of Muslim- friendly services. Access to halal food, mosques, and Muslim-friendly accommodations in non-Muslim regions is a decisive factor for travelers. Safe travel environments and clear signage indicating religious facilities can increase perceived comfort and encourage visitation. For Muslim tourists, reassurance about the ability to fulfill religious obligations while traveling significantly increases destination appeal. Promotion involves the communication strategies used to inform and persuade potential tourists. In halal tourism, culturally sensitive promotional campaigns that highlight compliance with Islamic values, family-friendliness, and religious accommodations are more likely to resonate with Muslim travelers. Digital platforms and social media, in particular, are effective in disseminating authentic, user-generated content and destination endorsements from fellow Muslims. Endorsements from Muslim influencers, the availability of Arabic or native language materials, and visual cues such as mosque imagery or halal logos can also enhance promotional effectiveness. The convergence of Muslim-friendly tourism, the theory of planned behavior, and the marketing mix provides a comprehensive framework for examining the behavioral intentions of Muslim travelers, particularly when they choose to visit non-Muslim destinations. Understanding how religiosity, attitudes, social norms, control perceptions, and marketing stimuli influence travel behavior provides theoretical and practical insights into how destinations can better serve and engage this rapidly growing market segment. 3. Materials and Methods This research employs a quantitative approach to examine the determinants of Muslim tourists’ intentions to visit non- Muslim destinations in Indonesia. The study is grounded in the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), which explains how attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control influence behavioral intentions. Data were collected through a structured online questionnaire distributed via social media platforms and Muslim travel community networks over 2 months. The study utilized a purposive sampling technique to ensure the inclusion of respondents who met specific criteria: (i) aged between 25 and 50 years, representing the most active travel segment; (ii) identifying as Muslim; and (iii) residing outside North Sulawesi, the focal non-Muslim destination area. The number of questionnaires filled out was 400, then after going through data screening and cleaning, the number of respondents used was 361. The questionnaire consisted of three main sections: demographic information, TPB constructs (attitude, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control, and intention), and marketing mix variables (product, price, place, and promotion). All measurement items were adapted from established scales in previous tourism and behavioral studies, modified to fit the context of halal and non-Muslim tourism. Respondents rated their agreement using a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Arif et al. (2026) 5 disagree to 5 = strongly agree). To ensure reliability and validity, a pilot test with 30 participants was conducted, and all constructs showed Cronbach’s alpha values above 0.70, indicating acceptable internal consistency. Data analysis was performed using Eviews version 13. Multiple regression analysis was applied to estimate the effects of the TPB components and marketing mix factors on travel intention. At the same time, diagnostic tests—such as normality, multicollinearity, and heteroscedasticity tests—were conducted to confirm model assumptions. Ethical considerations were observed throughout the research, including informed consent from all participants and adherence to institutional ethical standards approved by the university’s ethics committee. The research model used in this research is as follows: Intentioni = α + β1 Attitudei + β2 Normsi + β3 Behaviori + β4 Religiousityi + β5 Producti + β6 Pricei + β7 Placei + β8 Promotioni + εi where: Intention : intention of Muslim travellers Attitude : the attitudes of Muslim travellers Norms : norms subjective Behavior : perceived behavioral controls Religiousity : religiousity of Muslim travelers Product : the tourist destination Price : price or travel cost Place : location of tourist destination Promotion : the promotion of a tourist destination 4. Results and Discussion 4.1. Results Several main findings were obtained from this research. First, the factors influencing Muslim travelers' intentions to visit Muslim-friendly tourist destinations are attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavior control. Notably, religiosity does not affect Muslim travelers' intentions to visit Muslim-friendly destinations. The second finding was that the majority of respondents agreed that non-Muslim destinations such as North Sulawesi should be used as Muslim-friendly destinations. The third finding is that most respondents plan to visit North Sulawesi if the government designates it a Muslim-friendly tourist destination. The characteristics of the respondents in this research can be seen in Table 1. The number of respondents in this research was dominated by women (56%) and men (44%). On the basis of the age distribution of the respondents, the majority are dominated by the younger generation, both in the 20–30-year age range (36%) and 31–40-year-olds (31%). Meanwhile, the age range of 41--50% is only 27%, and the smallest is over 51 years old, namely, 5%. This result aligns with Aziz et al. (2018), who also reported that young adults demonstrated the highest levels of motivation to travel. The number of respondents who disagreed and were neutral was only 16%. This result shows high acceptance from the community if the government wants to expand Muslim-friendly tourist destinations not only in Muslim-majority areas but also in Muslim-minority areas. The results suggest that Muslim tourists are more inclined to visit destinations that offer adequate religious facilities, such as prayer rooms, ablution spaces, and clear information about halal food options (Alim et al., 2023; Juliana et al., 2023). This reflects the notion that attitudes are shaped by both the functional benefits of the destination and the emotional comfort of maintaining religious practices while traveling. Previous studies corroborate the finding that a positive attitude toward a destination increases travel intention (Akter & Hasan, 2023; Nguyen et al., 2023). For instance, Osman et al. (2024) emphasized that a positive travel attitude enhances not https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Arif et al. (2026) 7 only initial intention but also satisfaction and loyalty, which are vital for sustainable tourism development. Additionally, the respondents in this study expressed comfort when provided with accessible information about Muslim-friendly accommodations, such as Sharia-compliant hotels, echoing the importance of perceived destination readiness (Vegirawati et al., 2019; Syara & Fauzan, 2023). This suggests that destination managers should not only focus on the provision of facilities but also ensure the visibility and communication of such offerings, particularly for first-time visitors, who may rely heavily on pre-travel information. The accessibility of this information, whether via websites, mobile apps, or social media, enhances the perception of Muslim- friendliness and fosters positive attitudes that translate into increased visit intentions. In addition, attitudes impact tourists' satisfaction and loyalty (Osman et al., 2024). In addition, most respondents said that they would feel comfortable visiting tourist destinations that provided information about restaurants that provided halal food and drinks (Rahman et al., 2020; Hariani & Hanafiah, 2024). The government should provide information about restaurants that have halal certificates (Katuk et al., 2021). Subjective norms also significantly influence Muslim tourists’ intentions to visit non-Muslim destinations. This research uses several indicators to measure subjective norms. First, respondents believe that Muslim-friendly tourism benefits both tourists and the Muslim community in North Sulawesi. Thus, developing Muslim-friendly tourist destinations will increase tolerance among religious communities in North Sulawesi. Next, they developed Muslim-friendly tourist destinations in North Sulawesi as a form of religious moderation. Furthermore, all levels of society, regardless of religion, can benefit from the development of Muslim-friendly tourism in North Sulawesi. Finally, Muslim-friendly tourism in North Sulawesi will form an attitude of mutual respect between religious communities. Table 4 shows that subjective norms influence Muslim travelers' intentions to visit nonmuslim destinations. The analysis reveals that social approval and perceived communal benefits play important roles in shaping travel intentions. Specifically, the respondents perceived Muslim-friendly tourism in North Sulawesi as a catalyst for interfaith tolerance, religious moderation, and mutual respect. These findings align with those of previous studies, such as Ramadhani and Mochklas (2019), Erul et al. (2023), and Mohammed et al. (2023), which highlight the influence of social expectations and cultural norms on travel behavior. Interestingly, the community-centric narrative found in the responses emphasizing tolerance and inclusivity suggests that Muslim-friendly tourism is seen not only as a religious concern but also as a social good that benefits the broader society. This reframes subjective norms beyond the influence of family and peers to include broader sociocultural values, such as promoting peaceful coexistence and enhancing communal harmony. However, the findings diverge from those of Akter and Hasan (2023), who reported that subjective norms had no significant influence on Muslim travelers' intentions. This discrepancy may be attributed to contextual differences such as cultural background, level of religious diversity, or societal narratives about tourism. In regions such as North Sulawesi, where religious minorities coexist, the social function of tourism may carry additional weight in shaping perceptions and behaviors. In perceived behavioral control, several indicators are considered. First, respondents believe that their level of education affects their understanding of Muslim-friendly tourism. Second, the availability of Muslim-friendly facilities increases respondents' confidence in travelling to North Sulawesi. Third, respondents indicate that having sufficient funds is important for their travel plans to North Sulawesi. Fourth, having free time is also a factor in their decision to travel. Ultimately, the respondents believe that enhancing the roles of religious institutions and tourism stakeholders is crucial for developing Muslim- friendly tourist destinations in North Sulawesi. The empirical results in Table 4 confirm that perceived behavioral control affects the intentions of Muslim travelers, which aligns with previous studies that highlighted its impact on travel intentions. These findings align with prior research showing that when travelers feel empowered and capable of practicing their religion comfortably, they are more likely to follow through with travel intentions (Akter & Hasan, 2023; Bui, 2023; Erul et al., 2023; Grady & Sihombing, 2022; Lestari et al., 2023; Nguyen et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022). The findings suggest that, in this context, the PBC is shaped not only by individual agency (e.g., having funds or time) but also by structural enablers, such as the presence of Islamic infrastructure and the support of religious institutions. The inclusion of stakeholders such as mosques, Islamic organizations, and tourism boards is therefore crucial to improving Muslim tourists’ confidence in visiting non-Muslim destinations. In this context, strengthening collaboration between religious institutions and tourism authorities could further enhance Muslim-friendly infrastructure and services. One of the most notable and somewhat unexpected findings is that religiosity does not have a significant direct effect on Muslim travelers’ intentions to visit non-Muslim destinations. This result contradicts several studies that identify religiosity as a key determinant in travel behavior (Rahman et al., 2021; Liat et al., 2021; Sudarsono et al., 2021; Juliana et al., 2023). However, it aligns with Aji et al. (2021), who argue that religiosity may not influence travel decisions directly but rather indirectly through attitudes and perceptions of destination risk. To measure religiosity, this research uses several indicators. First, respondents believe that Islamic law governs all aspects of life. Second, they prefer to stay in hotels that are Muslim friendly. Third, they avoid consuming food and drinks prohibited in Islam. Mohammed et al. (2023) suggested that halal attitudes, values, and safety have a positive influence on tourists' intentions to visit destinations. Fourth, respondents emphasize the importance of having a prayer room available while https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Arif et al. (2026) 8 travelling (Said et al., 2022; Saville & Mahbubi, 2021). Fifth, respondents have a clear understanding of what is permissible and prohibited in Islamic law. Juliana et al. (2023) recommended that the government enhance halal infrastructure to promote the development of Muslim-friendly tourism. The indicators used to measure religiosity in this study reflect a high level of spiritual awareness among respondents. However, these values did not translate into an outright rejection of non-Muslim destinations. This may suggest a pragmatic orientation among Muslim travelers, who are willing to visit non-Muslim destinations provided that certain religious needs are met. In other words, destination readiness may moderate the influence of religiosity. Another explanation could be the emergence of a more adaptive and global-minded segment of Muslim tourists who, while devout, are open to intercultural experiences as long as basic religious accommodations are available. These travelers may separate core religious values from destination labels, focusing more on functionality (e.g., the presence of halal food and prayer spaces) than on whether a destination is a Muslim majority or not. This finding encourages destination managers in non-Muslim regions to focus less on religious identity politics and more on tangible service provisions. It also suggests that religiosity should be treated as a moderating or mediating variable in future models rather than a straightforward predictor of travel intention. The inclusion of the marketing mix in the analysis enriches the behavioral framework by highlighting how destination management strategies influence traveler intention. This study confirms that the marketing mix comprising product, price, place, and promotion significantly influences tourists' intentions to visit Muslim-friendly destinations. Each element plays a vital role in shaping perceptions, satisfaction, and ultimately, the decision to travel. This research revealed that products influence tourists' intentions to visit a Muslim-friendly tourist destination. The context of Muslim-friendly tourism includes the availability of halal-certified food, Sharia-compliant accommodations, prayer facilities, and recreational offerings that align with Islamic values. This finding supports the argument of Battour and Ismail (2016), who assert that halal-compliant products and services form the foundation of Muslim-friendly tourism appeals. Their research suggests that destinations offering a holistic and well-integrated package of halal amenities are more likely to attract Muslim tourists. Similarly, Eid and El-Gohary (2014) emphasized that the perceived value of such products enhances tourists’ satisfaction and fosters repeat visitation. In line with this, Nuzulia (2021) revealed that destination image and service quality further mediate travel intentions. Destination image encompasses cognitive and affective elements and has a strong, positive relationship with Muslim tourists' travel intentions (Dabphet, 2021; Preko et al., 2022). Moreover, Mursid and Anoraga (2022) reported that halal destination attributes significantly impact perceived emotional and functional value, which in turn affects tourists' intention to revisit (Mursid, 2023). This underlines the importance of carefully managing a destination’s image through consistent branding and messaging strategies, especially when targeting the Muslim market (Nassar et al., 2015). Furthermore, service quality— particularly the availability of Muslim-friendly amenities such as halal food and daily prayer facilities—is a strong determinant of satisfaction and loyalty (Liat et al., 2021). When visiting non-Islamic destinations, Muslim tourists primarily seek halal food, water-friendly toilets, and prayer facilities (Suharko et al., 2018; Jia & Chaozhi, 2020). These preferences suggest that even non-Islamic destinations can expand their market by implementing inclusive strategies such as acquiring halal certifications, improving halal visibility in travel platforms, and offering accommodations that meet sharia compliance standards. Additionally, many Muslim travelers rely heavily on online reviews, recommendations from friends, and travel platforms to inform their decisions (Melo & Farias, 2014; Adel et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2022). Among younger demographics in particular, the use of technology and social media plays a central role in evaluating the availability of halal services and forming travel intentions (Berakon et al., 2023). The price or cost of travel is one of the key factors that determines whether an individual will visit a Muslim-friendly tourist attraction. This study indicates that the perceived affordability of travel has a direct relationship with a tourist’s intention to visit. If costs related to flights, accommodations, food, and other travel-related services are perceived as excessive, they can significantly deter intention. Hidayat et al. (2021) reported that price significantly influences tourists' decisions to stay at three- and four-star hotels, highlighting the importance of affordable pricing in attracting Muslim tourists. This study highlights the importance of tourism providers offering value-for-money services to attract budget-conscious travelers. Price is a crucial factor in Muslim tourists' decision-making processes, and it often interacts with other key elements, such as quality, halal compliance, and emotional experiences. Therefore, tourism providers aiming to attract Muslim tourists should consider a holistic approach that combines competitive pricing with high-quality, halal-compliant services to influence tourists' intentions to visit effectively. he interaction between price and other variables, such as service quality and emotional experiences, suggests that a comprehensive pricing strategy, rather than mere cost-cutting, is essential for attracting and retaining Muslim tourists. In the context of Muslim-friendly tourism, the place element encompasses not only the geographical location of a destination but also its accessibility, availability of halal facilities, and overall environment, which aligns with Islamic principles. These factors significantly influence the travel intentions of Muslim tourists. Yusuf et al. (2021) highlighted that perceptions of access, communication, the environment, and service are significant factors influencing tourists' intentions. Specifically, Islamic https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Arif et al. (2026) 9 environmental factors such as gender-segregated facilities, visible religious symbols, and culturally appropriate entertainment substantially increase the comfort level and appeal of the destination. Similarly, Primadona et al. (2024) performed a systematic literature review focusing on West Nusa Tenggara (NTB), Indonesia. Their research identified the availability of halal food, halal accommodations, and the sociocultural environment as key factors influencing tourists' intentions to visit halal destinations. The study emphasized that the physical and cultural aspects of a location play crucial roles in attracting Muslim tourists. These findings reinforce the need for destination managers to not only provide physical infrastructure but also foster a cultural atmosphere that respects and promotes Islamic values. Promotion, as a component of the marketing mix, plays a pivotal role in shaping tourists' intentions, particularly within the context of Muslim-friendly tourism. Effective promotional strategies can enhance awareness, build trust, and influence the decision-making process of Muslim travelers. Hanafiah and Ahmad (2021) reported that marketing promotions significantly influence tourists' attitudes, which in turn affect their intention to visit. This study underscores the importance of targeted promotional efforts in attracting Muslim millennial travelers. Promotion, particularly through digital and social media channels, significantly influences Muslim tourists' intentions to visit Muslim-friendly destinations. Effective promotional strategies that resonate with the values and preferences of Muslim travelers can enhance destination appeal and influence travel decisions. This aligns with the digital consumption patterns of Muslim millennials and Gen Z travelers, who often seek reassurance about halal compatibility through blogs, vlogs, social media influencers, and travel forums. Crafting narratives that resonate with these values and disseminate them via trusted channels can enhance destination image and credibility, making destinations more attractive to this growing market segment. In addition to digital media, word-of-mouth marketing, especially peer recommendations from other Muslim travelers, serves as a powerful tool. Satisfied tourists who experience genuine hospitality and halal-compliant services are likely to become informal ambassadors, promoting the destination organically. To support such promotion, local and national governments can play a strategic role by investing in branding, certification systems, and incentives for halal-friendly service providers. Operators of Muslim-friendly tourism destinations should seek support from both central and local governments while focusing on enhancing and sustaining positive tourist experiences. Increasing the number of small-scale halal ventures, securing government support for halal tourism infrastructure, promoting word-of-mouth referrals, and offering discounted halal services can benefit cities (Isa et al., 2018; Huda et al., 2022). Increasing the understanding of Islamic attributes can improve tourist satisfaction at Muslim-friendly destinations (Ilisa et al., 2020). Tourism managers should align their offerings with the specific needs of Muslim travelers (Hassani & Moghavvemi, 2019). The government must standardize Muslim-friendly tourism to ensure that all such destinations meet consistent service quality standards (Pamukcu & Sariisik, 2021; Samori & Sabtu, 2014), thereby enhancing destination competitiveness (Lestari et al., 2023). Destination authorities must also increase the accessibility of halal-related information, as tourists frequently rely on such data to assess whether destinations meet their religious needs (Dagustani et al., 2018). Ultimately, the development of Muslim-friendly tourism cannot be achieved in isolation. It requires a multistakeholder approach involving tourism operators, government institutions, religious organizations, and the private sector. Only through collaboration and a shared understanding of Muslim tourist needs spanning tangible services and intangible cultural values can destinations achieve long-term success. This study contributes to the growing body of literature by demonstrating that the 4Ps of marketing are not only applicable to general tourism behavior but also particularly salient in shaping the travel intentions of Muslim tourists. 5. Conclusion This study investigates the key determinants influencing Muslim travelers' intentions to visit non-Muslim destinations. The findings reveal that several factors—namely, attitudes, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control, and the marketing mix elements of product, price, place, and promotion—significantly shape the travel intentions of Muslim tourists. Interestingly, religiosity was found to have no statistically significant effect on such intentions, suggesting that practical considerations and external influences may play a more prominent role in travel decision-making than previously assumed. Furthermore, the majority of the respondents expressed a positive attitude toward the government's initiative to expand Muslim-friendly tourism into non-Muslim-majority regions. They indicated a willingness to visit these destinations if they were officially recognized and promoted as accommodating halal-conscious travelers. These insights highlight a growing demand for inclusive tourism practices that respect and facilitate diverse cultural and religious needs. In light of these findings, the global tourism industry must adopt more inclusive, adaptive, and sustainable strategies that cater to the unique expectations of Muslim travelers. This includes providing access to accurate halal-related information, improving visibility and trust in halal-certified services, and fostering an environment where Muslim tourists can comfortably fulfil their religious obligations while travelling. Halal certification plays a critical role in this regard, acting as a bridge that aligns tourism offerings with Islamic principles, particularly in non-Muslim destinations. On the basis of the research findings, several policy recommendations are proposed. First, the government should develop infrastructure to support Muslim-friendly tourism in non-Muslim destinations, as current facilities for worship are https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Arif et al. (2026) 10 lacking, and travelers may need to seek permission to pray at local residences. This includes providing accessible and designated prayer spaces, wudu (ablution) facilities, and clearly marked signage, thereby reducing the burden on travelers, who currently must seek ad hoc arrangements for religious observances. Second, providing information or guidebooks for Muslim travelers, including details on mosques, halal restaurants, sharia-compliant hotels, and tourist attractions in non-Muslim destinations, is necessary. These should include directories of halal-certified restaurants, sharia-compliant accommodations, nearby mosques or musallas, and relevant local cultural insights, enabling travelers to plan confidently and enjoyably. Third, the government should educate travel agents and promote Muslim-friendly tour packages. Equipping them with the knowledge to design and promote Muslim-friendly packages will help align travel services with the values and expectations of this growing market segment. Fourth, support should be given to culinary establishments to obtain halal certification. This includes streamlining the certification process, providing financial or technical assistance where necessary, and integrating certified venues into official tourism marketing platforms. JSON: Name: muslim_nonmuslim_travel_intent Title: Multiple-regression and structural-equation analysis of determinants of Muslim travelers' intention to visit non-Muslim tourist destinations in Indonesia Short Hypothesis: Increased scores on attitude, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control, and each marketing-mix dimension (product, price, place, promotion) cause higher intention among Muslim travelers to visit non-Muslim tourist destinations, while individual religiosity has no significant direct effect on intention. Related Work: Prior research on Muslim-friendly or halal tourism has primarily used survey-based quantitative methods grounded in the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) and individual marketing-mix components. Existing studies demonstrate that attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control predict travel intention in many contexts, and that product/price/place/promotion elements correlate with destination choice. However, limitations remain: most work focuses on Muslim-majority destinations or cross-country comparisons rather than on within-country non-Muslim destinations; religiosity has been measured inconsistently and its role is ambiguous (direct predictor versus moderator/mediator); many analyses rely on single-equation regressions without latent-variable modelling or rigorous causal checks; common method bias, sampling biases (convenience or purposive samples), and cross-sectional designs limit causal inference and generalizability; standardized measures for destination halal-readiness and marketing inputs are lacking; and few studies compare predictive models (e.g., regression versus machine learning) or perform ablation/robustness tests to isolate the incremental value of marketing-mix variables over TPB constructs. Abstract: This research addresses which psychological and marketing factors determine Indonesian Muslim travelers' intention to visit non-Muslim tourist destinations. We propose a quantitative pipeline that integrates the Theory of Planned Behavior (attitude, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control) with a four-parameter marketing-mix (product, price, place, promotion) and an explicit religiosity measure. The approach combines confirmatory factor analysis, multiple linear regression, and structural equation modeling for latent-variable estimation, supplemented by predictive baselines (regularized regression and tree-based models) and cross-validated out-of-sample evaluation. The main contribution is a reproducible experimental protocol that quantifies the relative and incremental explanatory power of TPB versus marketing-mix predictors and tests the direct effect of religiosity on intention. Expected outcomes include ranked effect sizes, model comparison statistics, and robustness checks (subgroup analyses and assumption diagnostics) that clarify whether marketing interventions or psychological constructs are stronger levers for increasing visit intention in non-Muslim regional contexts. Results will inform destination management and generate generalizable evidence on models of halal-friendly tourism demand. Experiments: Datasets: 1) Primary survey: structured questionnaire administered to n=800 Indonesian Muslim respondents aged 18-60, stratified by region, gender, and urban/rural status; items: validated multi-item scales for attitude (4 items), subjective norms (3 items), perceived behavioral control (4 items), religiosity (5-item scale), marketing-mix subscales (product 5 items, price 3 items, place 4 items, promotion 4 items), intention (3 items). Responses on 5-point Likert scales. 2) Secondary destination features: administrative indicators per destination (presence of prayer facilities, halal-certified restaurants count, distance to transport hub). Baselines: A) TPB-only linear model (OLS) predicting continuous intention; B) Marketing-mix-only OLS; C) Full OLS (TPB + marketing-mix + religiosity + controls); D) Regularized linear model (elastic net) on same covariates; E) Random forest regressor for predictive benchmark; F) Structural equation model (SEM) estimating latent constructs and direct/indirect effects. Evaluation metrics: adjusted R-squared, out-of-sample R-squared from 10-fold cross-validation, RMSE, standardized regression coefficients with p-values, AIC/BIC for model comparison, variable importance (for random forest), comparative fit indices for SEM (CFI, TLI, RMSEA), and nested-model F-tests. Experimental setup: preprocess by mean-centering and checking Cronbach's alpha >=0.70 for each scale; perform confirmatory factor analysis to validate measurement model; run OLS and elastic net with k-fold CV (k=10) and hyperparameter grid search for regularization; train random forest with 500 trees and max depth tuned by CV; conduct SEM with bootstrapped (5,000) confidence intervals for path coefficients. Ablation and comparisons: 1) Ablation A: remove marketing-mix block to measure incremental R-squared of TPB alone; 2) Ablation B: remove TPB block to measure incremental R-squared of marketing-mix alone; 3) Ablation C: drop religiosity to assess change in coefficients and fit; 4) Test mediation: whether attitudes mediate the effect of promotion/product on intention using bootstrapped indirect effect tests; 5) Subgroup analyses: estimate models separately by age group (18-30, 31-45, 46-60), gender, and prior international travel experience. Robustness checks: VIF for multicollinearity, White test for heteroskedasticity, Durbin-Wu-Hausman test for endogeneity using instrument candidates (distance to nearest large mosque as instrument for perceived place), and sensitivity of results to alternative binary outcome specification (intention >3) evaluated with logistic regression and AUC. Risk Factors and Limitations: Measurement error in self-reported Likert items and social desirability bias; common method variance due to single-source cross-sectional survey; sampling bias from nonresponse or imperfect stratification reducing representativeness; limited external validity beyond Indonesian contexts and specific non-Muslim destinations; inability of cross-sectional models to establish causality (reverse causation and omitted variable bias); potential endogeneity of marketing-mix perceptions (simultaneity between intention and perceived destination attributes); multicollinearity among predictors (TPB constructs correlated with marketing variables) reducing coefficient interpretability; limited power for subgroup analyses if effective sample sizes are small; inaccuracies or incompleteness in secondary administrative indicators for halal-readiness; SEM and bootstrap inference require moderate compute but may scale poorly with very large item sets; results may not generalize to differing cultural or legal environments where halal certification or religious norms operate differently.
